newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania, Slovenia press on with NATO drive.
newsitem.headline: Romania, Slovenia press on with NATO drive.

text.p: Disappointed Romania and Slovenia vowed on Thursday to battle on with campaigns to persuade the United States to back their longshot bids for quick admission to an expanded NATO.

The U.S. administration passed over both countries in announcing at a NATO meeting in Brussels that it favoured initial enlargement to include only three former Communist countries -- Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic.
"This decision does not protect sufficiently U.S. interests in this region," Romanian Foreign Minister Adrian Severin told a news conference in Bucharest.

Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea, who leaves for Washington next week to lobby support in the U.S. Senate, said Romania had not given up hope of first-round admission at next month's NATO summit in Madrid.
"We believe the final decision will be taken by consensus in Madrid," he told reporters. "We will continue to play our cards until the end and we won't stop until the summit."
In Ljubljana, Slovenian Foreign Minister Zoran Thaler said his former Yugoslav republic had the backing to try to engineer a change of heart in Washington.

"Slovenia enjoys the support of at least nine NATO member nations for its candidature," Thaler said in a statement issued by the Slovenian news agency STA. "This support is getting stronger and other members are not opposed to our bid."

U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen said President Bill Clinton was firm in wanting to limit the invitations to the three favoured countries. Romania and Slovenia, he said, were solid candidates for future expansion rounds.

Italy, a staunch supporter of both countries, disagreed with the U.S. decision as did Luxembourg. Italian Foreign Minister Beniamino Andreatta said he would try to persuade NATO members to broaden the invitation. French officials made no comment but Paris is Romania's biggest backer.

Severin suggested Washington could yet be swayed. "The final formula of NATO's first-wave expansion will only be known at Madrid," he said. "By then, we are sure that the U.S. administration will take into consideration all the pertinent arguments in our favour."
A Romanian Foreign Ministry statement said that as far as Bucharest was concerned "it is not the final decision of the United States, nor is it NATO's final decision".

Romania's centrist leaders, who won power in last November's election after seven years of rule by ex-communists, have led a high-profile campaign portraying Romanian membership as the best way to secure NATO's southern flank.
President Emil Constantinescu meets German Chancellor Helmut Kohl in Bonn on July 2 seeking last-minute support.

Western commentators say Slovenia, the most advanced of former communist states, meets membership criteria by virtue of its solid democratic institutions, respect for human rights, civilian control over the army and market economic strcutrues.
But Slovenia's largely undeveloped armed forces have little to offer NATO. The country had no navy or air force when it won independence from Yugoslavia in 1991.
